appraisal_events.evidence: « Je savais que moi seul pouvais dire de cette façon-là "Albertine" à Andrée. Et pourtant pour Albertine, pour Andrée, et pour moi-même, je sentais que je n'étais rien. Et je comprenais l'impossibilité où se heurte l'amour. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator raises the one token of possession he holds — the exclusively possessive way he can pronounce Albertine's name, envied earlier in Swann — and immediately annuls it, declaring himself nothing to Albertine, to Andrée and to himself; the surrounding meditation on jealousy, lying and the unreachable points of another's existence endorses this self-diminishment as the passage's governing judgment.

appraisal_events.evidence: « "Ah !" fit Andrée d'une voix fort ennuyée et comme effrayée de mon audace, qui ne fit du reste que s'en affermir » ; puis « Cela m'a fait grand plaisir d'entendre votre voix », donnée comme « l'enjolivement de phrases spéciales, comme jadis autour des "thés" »
appraisal_events.explanation: In the telephone exchange Andrée flinches at the narrator's proposal to come along — her dismay only hardens his resolve — and she covers by yielding and offering a closing pleasantry that the narrator explicitly glosses as a mere conventional ornament of telephone usage, so her warmth is locally emptied out and her position weakened.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator ends the passage having lost even the illusion of possessing Albertine: his surveillance call yields nothing (she will go to the Verdurins anyway) and he states outright that he is nothing to anyone, including himself.

His attempt to steer Albertine away from Mme Verdurin's must be conducted by proxy, is interrupted by Françoise and by the telephone operator, and is answered by the flat fact that Albertine is going regardless, leaving him without leverage in the exchange.
Andrée is locally lowered by being shown annoyed and alarmed at the narrator's audacity, yielding rather than refusing, and closing with a politeness the narrator treats as a hollow formula.

ambiguities: The recalled Swann/Odette anecdote (« Venez voir Odette ») looks at first like an elevation of Swann through the enviable possessive force of a first name, but the following paragraph retracts it — such mainmise is either indifferent or turns « les douceurs en douleurs » — so it is read here as ironized recollection feeding the narrator's self-diminishment rather than as a standalone elevation of Swann.

Andrée's closing « Cela m'a fait grand plaisir d'entendre votre voix » could be read as genuine warmth; the narrator's own gloss framing it as a conventional telephone ornament is what tips E2 negative, and without that gloss the exchange would be closer to a neutral report.
